_meta.description: A Lisp interpreter built in C++ from scratch — lexer, parser, evaluator, environments, closures, tail-call optimization, and mark-and-sweep garbage collection.
_meta.note: TWO FILES GOVERN EVERY LESSON. BOTH ARE REQUIRED. NEITHER OVERRIDES THE OTHER. (1) THIS FILE — CURRICULUM.json — is the authoritative lab index. It defines what each lab teaches, what is visible at the end, and what concepts must be taught via the tags field. Every tag is a teaching obligation. (2) LISP-CPP-LESSON-CONTRACT.md — contains the mandatory concept block template, the 9 laws, the naming rules, the lesson structure, and the self-check the AI must pass before submitting any lesson. An AI writing any lesson must read both files before writing a single word.

format.title: ConceptName — What This Lab Adds
format.concept: The single primary concept this lab introduces — one sentence
format.tags: Every concept that appears in this lab's code or explanation. Every tagged concept gets a full concept block in this lab. Tags are teaching obligations, not a first-appearance registry.
format.visibleAtEnd: Exact observable result when the lab is complete.

_meta.teachingRule: Every tag in a lab entry is a teaching obligation. The AI must write a full concept block for every tag before writing the code that uses it. No tag may appear in a lab without a concept block. No concept block may be skipped because the concept appeared in an earlier lab.

LAB-00.title: Toolchain — C++ Compiler, Build System, First Binary
LAB-00.concept: A C++ program is compiled to a native binary by a toolchain: the compiler translates source to machine code, the linker assembles it into an executable.
LAB-00.visibleAtEnd: Terminal prints 'Lisp interpreter v0.1' from a compiled and linked C++ binary built with CMake.

LAB-01.title: Memory Model — Stack, Heap, and Pointers
LAB-01.concept: C++ has two memory regions: the stack (automatic, short-lived, limited size) and the heap (manual, long-lived, unlimited) — every data structure decision flows from this.
LAB-01.visibleAtEnd: Program prints the memory address of a stack variable and a heap-allocated integer, then frees it — no memory leak reported by Valgrind or AddressSanitizer.

LAB-02.title: Structs and Enums — Modeling Data Without Classes
LAB-02.concept: A struct groups related data under one name; an enum gives a finite set of named integer constants — together they are the foundation of every data model in C.
LAB-02.visibleAtEnd: Program creates a Token struct with a type enum field, prints its tag and value — the exact structure the lexer will use.

LAB-03.title: std::vector and std::string — The Two Containers You Need First
LAB-03.concept: std::vector is a heap-allocated, resizable array that manages its own memory; std::string is a vector of chars — both abstract away manual memory management for linear sequences.
LAB-03.visibleAtEnd: Program stores a vector of Token structs built from a hardcoded string and prints each token — the raw output of what will become the lexer.

LAB-04.title: Functions — The Substitution Model in C++
LAB-04.concept: A function call in C++ replaces the call site with the function body, substituting arguments for parameters — the same substitution model SICP describes, now visible at the machine level.
LAB-04.visibleAtEnd: Program evaluates (+ 3 4) by hand using three C++ functions (add, eval_number, eval_plus) — no parsing yet, structure hardcoded — and prints 7.

LAB-05.title: Lexer — Turning Characters Into Tokens
LAB-05.concept: A lexer (lexical analyzer) reads a stream of characters and groups them into tokens — the smallest meaningful units of the language — before any meaning is assigned.
LAB-05.visibleAtEnd: tokenize("(+ 1 2)") prints: LPAREN PLUS NUMBER(1) NUMBER(2) RPAREN — one token per line, correctly classified.

LAB-06.title: Recursive Data — Building a Tree With Pointers
LAB-06.concept: A tree is a recursive data structure: each node contains data and pointers to child nodes of the same type — the only way to represent nested structure in memory.
LAB-06.visibleAtEnd: Program builds the AST for (+ 1 2) manually using Node* pointers and prints it as a indented tree: (+ \n  1 \n  2).

LAB-07.title: Parser — Turning Tokens Into a Tree
LAB-07.concept: A recursive descent parser reads tokens left-to-right and builds a tree by calling itself recursively whenever it encounters a nested structure — the recursion in the code mirrors the recursion in the data.
LAB-07.visibleAtEnd: parse(tokenize("(+ (* 2 3) 4)")) produces a correct nested AST printed as: (+ (* 2 3) 4) — two levels of nesting correctly parsed.

LAB-08.title: Evaluator — Walking the Tree
LAB-08.concept: The evaluator is a recursive function that pattern-matches on node type and computes a value — for numbers it returns the number, for lists it evaluates the operator and applies it to evaluated operands.
LAB-08.visibleAtEnd: eval(parse(tokenize("(+ (* 2 3) (- 10 4))"))) prints 12 — a nested arithmetic expression fully evaluated through a tree walk.

LAB-09.title: Lisp Values — The Tagged Union (Sum Type)
LAB-09.concept: A Lisp value can be a number, a symbol, a boolean, nil, or a list — a tagged union (also called a sum type) represents 'one of several types' in a single C++ struct using a type tag and a union.
LAB-09.visibleAtEnd: A LispVal struct represents numbers, symbols, and nil correctly — print_val(make_number(42)) prints '42', print_val(make_symbol("x")) prints 'x', print_val(NIL) prints 'nil'.

LAB-10.title: Environment — Scope as a Linked Chain
LAB-10.concept: An environment maps names to values; environments are linked in a chain — looking up a name searches the current frame, then the parent, matching exactly how lexical scope works at runtime.
LAB-10.visibleAtEnd: An Environment with a parent correctly resolves x from the parent when the child has no binding: define x=10 in parent, look up x in child — prints 10.

LAB-11.title: Define and Lookup — Variables in the Evaluator
LAB-11.concept: Extending the evaluator to handle (define x 5) stores a binding in the current environment; evaluating a symbol performs a lookup — together these make the language stateful.
LAB-11.visibleAtEnd: eval sequence: (define x 10), (define y 20), (+ x y) — evaluator correctly resolves x and y from the environment and prints 30.

LAB-12.title: Lambda — Functions as First-Class Values
LAB-12.concept: A lambda creates a function value that captures the environment it was defined in — the function is not called immediately, it is stored as a value and called later, carrying its scope with it.
LAB-12.visibleAtEnd: ((lambda (x) (* x x)) 5) evaluates to 25 — a lambda defined inline, applied immediately, parameter bound in a child environment, body evaluated.

LAB-13.title: Closures — Capturing the Environment
LAB-13.concept: A closure is a function paired with the environment that was active when it was created — it can access variables from its defining scope even after that scope has returned.
LAB-13.visibleAtEnd: (define make-adder (lambda (n) (lambda (x) (+ x n)))) — (define add5 (make-adder 5)) — (add5 3) prints 8. n is captured in add5's closure and still accessible.

LAB-14.title: If and Conditionals — Control Flow as a Value
LAB-14.concept: In Lisp, (if condition then else) is a special form that evaluates to a value — unlike C++ if statements, it is an expression, and only one branch is ever evaluated.
LAB-14.visibleAtEnd: (if (= 1 1) "yes" "no") prints yes. (if (= 1 2) "yes" "no") prints no. (if #f 0 (/ 1 0)) prints error from else branch, confirming only one branch evaluated.

LAB-15.title: Recursion — How the Call Stack Grows
LAB-15.concept: Every recursive function call pushes a new frame onto the C++ call stack — too many nested calls exhaust the stack, producing a stack overflow, which is a fundamental limit of the call-stack model.
LAB-15.visibleAtEnd: (define fact (lambda (n) (if (= n 0) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1)))))) — (fact 10) prints 3628800. (fact 10000) crashes with a stack overflow — the problem that motivates the next lab.

LAB-16.title: Tail Calls — Recursion Without Stack Growth
LAB-16.concept: A tail call is a function call that is the very last operation in a function — the caller's stack frame is no longer needed, so it can be reused instead of stacked, turning recursion into iteration.
LAB-16.visibleAtEnd: (define fact-iter (lambda (n acc) (if (= n 0) acc (fact-iter (- n 1) (* n acc))))) — (fact-iter 100000 1) completes without stack overflow. The stack stays flat.

LAB-17.title: Smart Pointers — RAII and Ownership
LAB-17.concept: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) ties a resource's lifetime to a C++ object's scope — std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr implement RAII for heap memory, eliminating manual delete.
LAB-17.visibleAtEnd: Refactored AST nodes use std::unique_ptr — AddressSanitizer reports zero memory leaks on a complete parse-and-eval cycle. The delete keyword does not appear in the codebase.

LAB-18.title: Garbage Collection — Mark and Sweep
LAB-18.concept: A garbage collector automatically reclaims heap memory that is no longer reachable from any live variable — mark-and-sweep works in two passes: trace all reachable objects, then free the rest.
LAB-18.visibleAtEnd: The interpreter runs (define f (lambda (x) x)) in a loop 10000 times — GC fires automatically when the heap exceeds a threshold, old allocations are freed, memory stays bounded.

LAB-19.title: std::variant — Type-Safe Unions in Modern C++
LAB-19.concept: std::variant is the modern C++ replacement for the manual tagged union — it stores one of several types safely, enforces that only the active type is accessed, and eliminates the undefined behavior of raw unions.
LAB-19.visibleAtEnd: LispVal refactored from raw tagged union to std::variant<int64_t, double, bool, std::string, std::nullptr_t, std::vector<LispVal>> — all existing tests still pass.

LAB-20.title: Classes and Encapsulation — Hiding the Mechanism
LAB-20.concept: A class bundles data and the functions that operate on it into one unit, and access specifiers (public/private) enforce which parts callers can touch — encapsulation makes the internal representation changeable without breaking users.
LAB-20.visibleAtEnd: Environment refactored from a free-standing struct + functions into a class with private data — the same eval tests pass, but the hash map is inaccessible from outside the class.

LAB-21.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism — One Interface, Many Behaviors
LAB-21.concept: Inheritance lets a derived class share structure from a base class; virtual functions let the caller invoke the derived class's version through a base class pointer — the mechanism behind runtime polymorphism.
LAB-21.visibleAtEnd: A Callable base class with a virtual call() method is subclassed by LambdaFunc and BuiltinFunc — eval dispatches through the base pointer and the correct version runs for each type.

LAB-22.title: Templates — Generic Code Without Duplication
LAB-22.concept: A C++ template generates code for multiple types from a single definition at compile time — the compiler stamps out a separate version for each type used, with zero runtime overhead.
LAB-22.visibleAtEnd: A generic Result<T, E> template wraps either a success value or an error — eval returns Result<LispVal, std::string> instead of throwing exceptions, all call sites updated.

LAB-23.title: Error Handling — Exceptions vs. Result Types
LAB-23.concept: Exceptions unwind the call stack to the nearest catch block; Result types make errors explicit in the return type — each is a different philosophy about whether failure is exceptional or expected.
LAB-23.visibleAtEnd: Evaluating (/ 1 0) returns a LispError value printed as 'Error: division by zero' without crashing. Evaluating (car '()) returns 'Error: car of empty list'. The REPL continues after both.

LAB-24.title: REPL — Read-Eval-Print Loop
LAB-24.concept: A REPL is an interactive loop that reads one expression, evaluates it, prints the result, and loops — it is both how Lisp was originally used and a concrete demonstration of the eval/apply cycle running continuously.
LAB-24.visibleAtEnd: Terminal shows a '> ' prompt. User types (+ 1 2) and presses Enter. Terminal prints 3 and shows a new prompt. User types (define x 5) then (+ x 3) and gets 8. Ctrl+C exits cleanly.

LAB-25.title: Built-in Library — list, car, cdr, cons
LAB-25.concept: The core Lisp list operations (cons, car, cdr) are not syntactic — they are functions implemented in C++ and registered in the global environment, making them indistinguishable from user-defined functions at the Lisp level.
LAB-25.visibleAtEnd: (cons 1 (cons 2 (cons 3 '()))) prints (1 2 3). (car '(a b c)) prints a. (cdr '(a b c)) prints (b c). (list 1 2 3) prints (1 2 3).

LAB-26.title: Quasiquote — Code as Data
LAB-26.concept: Quasiquote (backtick) is a macro that produces a list with selective evaluation — it is the bridge between Lisp's code-as-data nature and the ability to construct code programmatically.
LAB-26.visibleAtEnd: (let ((x 5)) `(the value is ,x)) prints (the value is 5). The backtick form is expanded at read time into a list construction — show both the quasiquoted form and the equivalent cons expression.

LAB-27.title: Macros — Transforming Code Before Evaluation
LAB-27.concept: A macro receives its arguments unevaluated as raw syntax, transforms them into a new expression, and returns that expression to be evaluated — macros operate at the level of code structure, not values.
LAB-27.visibleAtEnd: (define-macro (my-and a b) `(if ,a ,b #f)) — (my-and #t #f) prints #f. (my-and #f (/ 1 0)) prints #f without evaluating the division — proving b was not evaluated.

LAB-28.title: File I/O — Loading Lisp Source Files
LAB-28.concept: Reading a file in C++ opens a stream that produces characters sequentially — feeding that stream to the lexer and parser lets the interpreter load and execute Lisp source files from disk.
LAB-28.visibleAtEnd: stdlib.lisp contains (define (square x) (* x x)) — running ./lisp stdlib.lisp then dropping into REPL, (square 7) prints 49. Source loaded from disk, bound in global environment.

LAB-29.title: Standard Library — Writing Lisp in Lisp
LAB-29.concept: Once the interpreter has lambda, define, if, and the core list operations, you can implement higher-order functions (map, filter, fold) in Lisp itself — the language bootstraps from a small C++ core.
LAB-29.visibleAtEnd: stdlib.lisp defines map, filter, and fold in pure Lisp. (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) '(1 2 3 4 5)) prints (1 4 9 16 25). No C++ changes needed — the library is written in the language itself.

LAB-30.title: Performance — Profiling and Measuring What Matters
LAB-30.concept: Profiling finds where a program actually spends time — the 80/20 rule of performance says 80% of runtime is in 20% of the code, and optimizing the wrong 80% is wasted effort.
LAB-30.visibleAtEnd: gprof output shows environment lookup is the hottest path. Replacing linear-search env lookup with std::unordered_map cuts fib(30) benchmark from Xms to Yms — measured before and after.
